concepts.def: A nucleotide made of the base adenine, the pentose sugar ribose and a chain of three phosphate groups. It is the molecule that distributes energy within cells: energy released from carbon compounds in cell respiration is used to make ATP, and ATP then supplies that energy to the processes that need it.

A molecule made of a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and one or more phosphate groups. Nucleotides are the monomers of DNA and RNA, but ATP is also a nucleotide, one in which ribose carries adenine and three phosphates.

The role ATP plays as the immediate, universal supplier of energy to reactions in the cell. ATP is suited to this because it is soluble in water and moves freely through the cytoplasm, is stable at cell pH until an enzyme hydrolyses it, cannot diffuse out through the plasma membrane, releases energy in an amount suited to single reactions, and is regenerated from ADP and phosphate within seconds. It is a short-term supply that is recycled continuously, not a long-term store.

Movement of a substance across a membrane against its concentration gradient by a protein pump, using energy from ATP. It is one of the principal uses of ATP in cells; passive processes such as diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis do not use ATP.

The synthesis of larger molecules from smaller ones, such as building polypeptides from amino acids, polysaccharides from monosaccharides or DNA from nucleotides. Anabolic reactions require an input of energy, which ATP supplies.

Movement of a whole cell (for example a sperm cell swimming, or a leucocyte crawling) or of components within a cell (for example chromosomes being moved to the poles during mitosis, or vesicles being transported along the cytoskeleton). All of these depend on motor proteins that use energy released by hydrolysis of ATP.

The reaction in which ATP reacts with water to form ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and a phosphate group. Energy is released, and in the cell this energy is coupled to a process that needs it. The amount released per ATP is sufficient for many tasks in the cell.

The synthesis of ATP by joining a phosphate group to ADP. This is a condensation reaction that requires an input of energy, supplied in cell respiration (and photosynthesis). ATP and ADP are therefore interconverted continuously: hydrolysis releases energy, synthesis stores it.

The controlled release of energy from carbon compounds (organic compounds) inside cells, used to produce ATP. It is a chemical process carried out by every living cell and is distinct from gas exchange.

The movement of gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide across a surface, for example between alveolar air and blood in the lungs or between the air and the cells of a leaf. It supplies oxygen for aerobic respiration and removes carbon dioxide, but it is not itself respiration.

A carbon compound whose oxidation releases energy for ATP production. Glucose and fatty acids are the principal substrates in most cells, but a wide range of carbon compounds, including other sugars, glycerol and amino acids, can be respired.

Respiration that requires oxygen. Glucose (or another substrate such as a fatty acid) is completely oxidized to carbon dioxide and water with a large yield of ATP. In humans the word equation with glucose is: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; the later reactions occur in the mitochondria, so mitochondria are required.

Respiration that does not use oxygen. In humans, glucose is converted to lactate with a small yield of ATP (glucose → lactate); no carbon dioxide is formed. Only carbohydrate can be used as the substrate. All of the reactions occur in the cytoplasm, so mitochondria are not required.

The three-carbon product of anaerobic cell respiration in humans, formed from pyruvate in the cytoplasm. It is the waste product that accumulates in muscle during intense exercise when oxygen supply is insufficient.

The organelle in which the oxygen-requiring stages of aerobic cell respiration take place, releasing most of the ATP that a eukaryotic cell produces. Mitochondria are required for aerobic respiration but not for anaerobic respiration, which is completed in the cytoplasm.

The amount of oxygen consumed (or carbon dioxide produced) per unit time, usually expressed per unit mass of tissue, for example in cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹. It is affected by variables such as temperature, availability of substrate and of oxygen, and pH, and is calculated by dividing the measured change in volume by the time taken and by the mass of tissue.

Apparatus for measuring the rate of respiration of living material. Carbon dioxide released is absorbed by an alkali such as potassium hydroxide, so the decrease in gas volume, followed by the movement of a drop of coloured liquid along a capillary tube, is due to oxygen being taken up. A control tube containing non-living material of the same volume shows the effect of any change in temperature or pressure.

The loss of electrons from a substance. In cell respiration this usually happens by removal of hydrogen atoms, each of which carries an electron, so a substrate that loses hydrogen (is dehydrogenated) has been oxidized. Gaining oxygen is also oxidation, but oxygen need not be involved.

The gain of electrons by a substance, in cell respiration usually by accepting hydrogen. Oxidation and reduction occur together as a redox reaction: when a substrate is oxidized by losing hydrogen, the carrier that accepts the hydrogen is reduced.

A coenzyme that acts as a hydrogen carrier in cell respiration. NAD accepts hydrogen (with electrons) removed from substrates and becomes reduced NAD; reduced NAD later gives up the electrons and is converted back to NAD, so a small pool of NAD is used over and over again.

Removal of hydrogen atoms from a substrate by a dehydrogenase enzyme. Because each hydrogen atom carries an electron, dehydrogenation oxidizes the substrate, and the hydrogen is passed to a carrier such as NAD.

The stepwise conversion of one glucose (6C) to two pyruvate (3C) in the cytoplasm, with no oxygen required. It involves phosphorylation of glucose using ATP, lysis (splitting) of the phosphorylated hexose into two three-carbon molecules, oxidation of these by dehydrogenation to form reduced NAD, and ATP formation. Each step is catalysed by a different enzyme.

The first stage of glycolysis, in which phosphate groups from two ATP molecules are added to glucose. This uses ATP rather than making it; it makes the sugar more reactive and unable to leave the cell.
Per glucose, glycolysis uses 2 ATP in phosphorylation and forms 4 ATP later, so the net yield is 2 ATP. It also forms 2 reduced NAD and 2 pyruvate.

Conversion of reduced NAD back to NAD so that glycolysis can continue. In anaerobic respiration in humans this is done by reducing pyruvate to lactate; no ATP is formed in this step, but it allows glycolysis to go on yielding a net two ATP per glucose.

Glycolysis followed by regeneration of NAD in which pyruvate is decarboxylated, releasing carbon dioxide, and the product is reduced to ethanol: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide. The pathway is the same as in humans up to pyruvate; only the NAD-regenerating step and therefore the final products differ. The carbon dioxide raises bread dough in baking and the ethanol is the alcohol in beer and wine in brewing.

The oxidation and decarboxylation of pyruvate (3C) in the mitochondrial matrix to form an acetyl group (2C), carbon dioxide and reduced NAD. The acetyl group is attached to coenzyme A, forming acetyl coenzyme A, which transfers it to the Krebs cycle.

A two-carbon acetyl group bound to the carrier molecule coenzyme A. Coenzyme A is not an enzyme: it carries acetyl groups, formed from pyruvate in the link reaction or from the breakdown of fatty acids, and hands them to oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle, being released to be reused.

Removal of a carboxyl group from a substrate as carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide released in aerobic respiration comes from decarboxylations in the link reaction and the Krebs cycle, not from a reaction of carbon with oxygen.

A cycle of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix in which the acetyl group (2C) from acetyl-CoA is transferred to oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C). Citrate is then converted back to oxaloacetate by a series of reactions that include two decarboxylations, releasing carbon dioxide, and four oxidations by dehydrogenation, most of which form reduced NAD; one ATP is formed directly per turn.
The six-carbon compound formed at the start of the Krebs cycle by transfer of a two-carbon acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to four-carbon oxaloacetate.
The four-carbon compound that accepts an acetyl group to form citrate and is regenerated by the reactions of the Krebs cycle, so it is not used up.

A series of electron carriers in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Reduced NAD (from glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle) transfers a pair of electrons to the first carrier, becoming NAD again; the electrons then pass from carrier to carrier, releasing energy at each transfer, until they reach oxygen.

A difference in hydrogen ion (proton) concentration across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Energy released as electrons flow along the electron transport chain is used to pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, so the intermembrane space becomes more concentrated in protons than the matrix.

The narrow space between the outer and inner membranes of the mitochondrion into which protons are pumped by the electron transport chain, and from which they flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase.

The use of a proton gradient across a membrane to drive ATP synthesis. Protons diffuse down their concentration gradient from the intermembrane space back into the matrix through ATP synthase, and the energy released is coupled to the phosphorylation of ADP.

An enzyme embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane that provides the only route for protons to flow back into the matrix. The flow of protons through it releases energy that it uses to join phosphate to ADP, forming ATP on the matrix side of the membrane.

The substance that accepts electrons from the last carrier of the electron transport chain. In aerobic respiration this is oxygen, which combines with the electrons and with protons from the matrix to form water. Without a terminal acceptor the carriers remain reduced and electron flow stops.

Water formed in aerobic respiration when oxygen accepts electrons from the electron transport chain and protons from the matrix. It is the fate of the oxygen consumed in respiration; the carbon dioxide released comes from decarboxylation, not from oxygen.

Fatty acids are broken down into two-carbon acetyl groups that enter aerobic respiration as acetyl-CoA and are oxidized in the Krebs cycle. Lipids yield roughly twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates because they contain less oxygen and more oxidizable hydrogen and carbon. Fatty acids cannot enter glycolysis, so they cannot be used in anaerobic respiration; glycolysis and anaerobic respiration occur only with carbohydrate as the substrate.

mcqs.q: Which statement about ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is correct?
options: It is a nucleotide: adenine and ribose joined to a chain of three phosphate groups.
It is a small protein that binds energy released from glucose in respiration.
It is the cell's main long-term reserve of energy, built up like glycogen.
It is destroyed once used and is rebuilt from glucose rather than from ADP.
mcqs.specStatementText: ATP carries energy from where it is released to where it is used
mcqs.explain: ATP is a nucleotide made of the base adenine, the pentose sugar ribose and three phosphate groups. It is the molecule that distributes energy within cells.
rationales: ATP is a nucleotide made of the base adenine, the pentose sugar ribose and three phosphate groups. It is the molecule that distributes energy within cells.

A student who files nucleotides under DNA only and thinks of ATP as a special protein picks this. In fact ATP is a nucleotide, not a protein, and energy is not 'bound' but released when ATP is hydrolysed.
A student who reads 'energy store' as a reserve for the future picks this. In fact a cell holds only a small pool of ATP and recycles it within seconds; long-term reserves are glycogen and lipid.
A student who pictures each ATP being made afresh from glucose picks this. In fact hydrolysis gives ADP and phosphate, and these are rejoined to re-form ATP; glucose supplies the energy, not the ADP.

mcqs.q: A cell needs an energy currency that can supply many different reactions in the cytoplasm. Which property makes ATP suitable for this role?
options: It holds a very large amount of energy, so that a cell can store it for many weeks between meals.
It releases energy in an amount suited to a single reaction and is quickly re-formed from ADP.
It is consumed after one use, so the cell then builds fresh ATP directly from glucose.
It acts as an enzyme, catalysing each of the reactions in the cytoplasm that need energy.
mcqs.specStatementText: ATP carries energy from where it is released to where it is used
mcqs.explain: ATP hydrolysis releases a modest packet of energy, enough for many individual tasks, and ADP is phosphorylated back to ATP within seconds, so a small pool of ATP can supply energy continuously.
rationales: A student who thinks ATP is a long-term store picks this. In fact ATP is used within seconds of being formed; energy for weeks is stored as glycogen and lipid, not as ATP.
ATP hydrolysis releases a modest packet of energy, enough for many individual tasks, and ADP is phosphorylated back to ATP within seconds, so a small pool of ATP can supply energy continuously.
A student who thinks ATP is used up and replaced from scratch picks this. In fact ATP is recycled: the ADP and phosphate formed by hydrolysis are rejoined using energy from respiration.
A student who thinks ATP is a protein or enzyme picks this. In fact ATP is a nucleotide; it supplies energy by being hydrolysed, and the reactions are catalysed by separate enzymes.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes a life process that ATP supplies with energy?
options: Water entering a root hair cell by osmosis uses ATP to cross the membrane against its gradient.
Joining amino acids into a polypeptide releases energy, which the cell holds as ATP.
Pumping sodium ions out of a neuron against their concentration gradient uses ATP directly.
Chromosomes move to the poles in mitosis without ATP, pulled by spindle fibres as they get shorter.
mcqs.specStatementText: What cells spend ATP on
mcqs.explain: Active transport across membranes is one of the principal uses of ATP: the sodium-potassium pump hydrolyses ATP to move ions against their concentration gradients.
rationales: A student who thinks every movement across a membrane needs ATP picks this. In fact osmosis is passive: water moves down its own gradient with no ATP hydrolysed.
A student who thinks bond-forming synthesis releases energy picks this. In fact synthesis of macromolecules (anabolism) requires energy, which ATP supplies; it does not produce ATP.
Active transport across membranes is one of the principal uses of ATP: the sodium-potassium pump hydrolyses ATP to move ions against their concentration gradients.
A student who reads mitosis diagrams as purely mechanical picks this. In fact movement of cell components such as chromosomes is driven by motor proteins that use energy from ATP.

mcqs.q: During a sprint, ATP in muscle fibres is hydrolysed and then re-formed thousands of times. Which statement about the energy transfers is correct?
options: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate needs an input of energy, and re-forming ATP releases it.
Hydrolysed ATP cannot be re-formed, so each contraction needs new ATP built from a glucose molecule.
The muscle takes energy directly from glucose during the sprint; hydrolysis of ATP is a minor side reaction.
Hydrolysis of ATP releases energy; energy from respiration is needed to re-form it from ADP.
mcqs.specStatementText: Hydrolysing ATP releases energy; making it takes energy in
mcqs.explain: Energy is released by hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate, and energy released from carbon compounds in respiration is required to synthesize ATP again from ADP and phosphate.
rationales: A student who merges 'respiration releases energy' with 'respiration makes ATP' reverses the direction and picks this. In fact energy is released by hydrolysis and required for synthesis.
A student who thinks ATP is consumed and replaced from scratch picks this. In fact the ADP and phosphate are rejoined; the same ADP molecules are recycled thousands of times during the sprint.

A student who remembers 'glucose releases energy for the cell' without ATP picks this. In fact contraction is powered by ATP hydrolysis; glucose supplies energy only through the ATP it is used to make.
Energy is released by hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate, and energy released from carbon compounds in respiration is required to synthesize ATP again from ADP and phosphate.

mcqs.q: A student writes: 'Cell respiration is when oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it in the lungs.' Which statement correctly evaluates this?
options: It is wrong: this describes gas exchange; cell respiration releases energy from carbon compounds to make ATP inside cells.
It is right: respiration is the exchange of gases at a respiratory surface, which the cells then make use of.
It is wrong: cell respiration is glucose reacting with oxygen inside cells, and glucose is the only substrate used.
It is wrong: cell respiration creates the energy a cell needs, using the oxygen that gas exchange brings into the body.
mcqs.specStatementText: Respiration makes ATP inside cells; gas exchange is something else
mcqs.explain: Gas exchange is the movement of gases across a surface. Cell respiration is a chemical process in every cell that releases energy from carbon compounds to produce ATP; the two must be distinguished.
rationales: Gas exchange is the movement of gases across a surface. Cell respiration is a chemical process in every cell that releases energy from carbon compounds to produce ATP; the two must be distinguished.

A student who uses the everyday meaning of 'respiration' as breathing picks this. In fact gas exchange supplies oxygen to and removes carbon dioxide from cells; respiration is what happens inside them.

A student who defines respiration by the glucose equation picks this. In fact glucose and fatty acids are the principal substrates, but a wide range of carbon compounds can be respired; the statement is wrong because it describes gas exchange, not because it omits glucose.

A student who thinks respiration creates energy picks this. In fact energy cannot be created; respiration releases energy already held in carbon compounds and transfers it to ATP, and the statement is wrong because it describes gas exchange.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes the substrates of cell respiration?
options: Only glucose can be respired, because it is the reactant in the equation for respiration.
Glucose and fatty acids are the main substrates, but many other carbon compounds can be used.
Glucose and fatty acids are the substrates, and either can be used with or without oxygen.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide are the substrates, since they are the substances exchanged at the lungs.
mcqs.specStatementText: Respiration makes ATP inside cells; gas exchange is something else
mcqs.explain: Glucose and fatty acids are the principal substrates for cell respiration, but a wide range of carbon (organic) compounds, including other sugars, glycerol and amino acids, can be respired.
rationales: A student who takes the glucose word equation as the definition of respiration picks this. In fact glucose is the standard example; a wide range of carbon compounds can be respired.
Glucose and fatty acids are the principal substrates for cell respiration, but a wide range of carbon (organic) compounds, including other sugars, glycerol and amino acids, can be respired.
A student who keeps substrates and oxygen requirement as separate lists picks this. In fact fatty acids can be respired only aerobically; only carbohydrate can be used anaerobically.

A student who confuses respiration with gas exchange picks the gases as substrates. In fact the substrate is a carbon compound; oxygen is a reactant in aerobic respiration but is not the source of the energy.

mcqs.q: Which statement about anaerobic cell respiration in humans is correct?
options: Glucose is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide, as it is in yeast cells.
Glucose is converted to lactate and carbon dioxide in the cytoplasm of the cell.
Glucose is converted to lactate, and no carbon dioxide is released at all.
Glucose is converted to lactate using a little oxygen rather than none.
mcqs.specStatementText: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans compared
mcqs.explain: The word equation is glucose → lactate. Anaerobic respiration in humans uses no oxygen, occurs in the cytoplasm, yields a little ATP and releases no carbon dioxide.
rationales: A student who confuses the human and yeast equations picks this. In fact humans convert glucose to lactate; ethanol and carbon dioxide are the products in yeast.
A student who thinks all respiration releases carbon dioxide picks this. In fact no carbon dioxide is released in human anaerobic respiration; the only product is lactate.
The word equation is glucose → lactate. Anaerobic respiration in humans uses no oxygen, occurs in the cytoplasm, yields a little ATP and releases no carbon dioxide.

A student who reads 'anaerobic' as 'low oxygen' picks this. In fact anaerobic respiration uses no oxygen at all; it consists only of glycolysis and lactate formation in the cytoplasm, so the oxygen-using reactions in the mitochondria play no part.

mcqs.q: Mature human red blood cells have no mitochondria. Which statement about cell respiration in these cells is correct?
options: They cannot respire at all, because all cell respiration takes place in mitochondria.
They respire anaerobically, and so they gain no ATP from the glucose they take up.
They respire anaerobically, releasing ethanol and carbon dioxide into the blood plasma.
They respire anaerobically in the cytoplasm, converting glucose to lactate.
mcqs.specStatementText: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans compared
mcqs.explain: Mitochondria are required for aerobic but not anaerobic respiration. Red blood cells respire anaerobically in the cytoplasm, with a small yield of ATP and lactate as the waste product.
rationales: A student who thinks every form of respiration is confined to mitochondria picks this. In fact glycolysis and lactate formation occur in the cytoplasm, so respiration continues without mitochondria.
A student who rounds the small anaerobic yield down to nothing picks this. In fact anaerobic respiration yields a net two ATP per glucose, which is enough for the needs of a red blood cell.
A student who applies the yeast equation to human cells picks this. In fact human cells convert glucose to lactate; they do not produce ethanol or carbon dioxide anaerobically.
Mitochondria are required for aerobic but not anaerobic respiration. Red blood cells respire anaerobically in the cytoplasm, with a small yield of ATP and lactate as the waste product.

mcqs.q: Aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule yields many times more ATP (roughly 30) than anaerobic respiration (2). Which statement explains the difference?
options: Without oxygen only glycolysis in the cytoplasm yields ATP; with oxygen the mitochondria release far more of the energy in glucose.
Both pathways run in the mitochondria, but without oxygen the mitochondria work more slowly and so make less ATP.
Without oxygen the cell converts glucose to ethanol, which keeps most of the energy, so much less ATP is made.
Without oxygen the cell uses the little oxygen dissolved in its cytoplasm, so only a small amount of ATP forms.
mcqs.specStatementText: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans compared
mcqs.explain: Anaerobic respiration ends with glycolysis and lactate formation in the cytoplasm, so most of the energy remains in the lactate. Aerobic respiration continues in the mitochondria, oxidizing the substrate completely and yielding far more ATP.
rationales: Anaerobic respiration ends with glycolysis and lactate formation in the cytoplasm, so most of the energy remains in the lactate. Aerobic respiration continues in the mitochondria, oxidizing the substrate completely and yielding far more ATP.
A student who places all respiration in mitochondria picks this. In fact anaerobic respiration does not use mitochondria at all; it is completed in the cytoplasm, where only glycolysis yields ATP.
A student who applies the yeast pathway to humans picks this. In fact human anaerobic respiration produces lactate, not ethanol, though it is true that most of the energy stays in the product.

A student who thinks anaerobic respiration means 'a little oxygen' picks this. In fact anaerobic respiration uses no oxygen; the low yield is because glycolysis alone releases only a small fraction of the energy.

mcqs.q: In a respirometer, carbon dioxide is absorbed by potassium hydroxide. With 5.0 g of germinating seeds, the gas volume in the apparatus fell by 1.2 cm³ in 10 minutes. What is the rate of respiration per gram?
options: 0.024 cm³ of carbon dioxide produced per gram per minute
0.024 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute
0.12 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute
0.024 cm³ of oxygen given out per gram per minute
mcqs.specStatementText: Measuring the rate of respiration
mcqs.explain: The fall in volume equals the oxygen consumed, because carbon dioxide is removed by the alkali. Rate = 1.2 cm³ ÷ 10 min ÷ 5.0 g = 0.024 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹.
rationales: A student who thinks the liquid is moved by carbon dioxide picks this. In fact the potassium hydroxide absorbs the carbon dioxide, so the volume change measures oxygen uptake.
The fall in volume equals the oxygen consumed, because carbon dioxide is removed by the alkali. Rate = 1.2 cm³ ÷ 10 min ÷ 5.0 g = 0.024 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹.
A student who divides by time but forgets to divide by the mass of seeds picks this. 1.2 ÷ 10 = 0.12 cm³ min⁻¹ for the whole 5.0 g sample; per gram this is 0.024.
A student who thinks plant material releases oxygen picks this. In fact germinating seeds respire and do not photosynthesize; the volume fell because oxygen was taken up, not released.

mcqs.q: A student measured oxygen uptake by yeast (cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹) at five temperatures: 20 °C 0.10; 30 °C 0.19; 40 °C 0.31; 50 °C 0.26; 60 °C 0.04. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Rate rises with temperature over the whole range, so the low reading at 60 °C must be an experimental error.
Above 40 °C the yeast switches to anaerobic respiration, which uses no oxygen, so oxygen uptake falls.
Rate rises with temperature up to an optimum near 40 °C, then falls as the enzymes of respiration denature.
At 60 °C the extra carbon dioxide produced expands and pushes the liquid back, hiding the true rate.
mcqs.specStatementText: Measuring the rate of respiration
mcqs.explain: Every stage of respiration is enzyme-catalysed. Rate increases with temperature until an optimum, then falls rapidly as enzymes denature, which matches the sharp drop between 50 °C and 60 °C.
rationales: A student who applies only the kinetic-energy explanation picks this. In fact the sharp fall from 50 °C to 60 °C is the expected effect of enzyme denaturation, not an error.
A student who uses 'switched to anaerobic' as a general explanation picks this. In fact oxygen was freely available; the fall is due to denaturation of the enzymes catalysing respiration.
Every stage of respiration is enzyme-catalysed. Rate increases with temperature until an optimum, then falls rapidly as enzymes denature, which matches the sharp drop between 50 °C and 60 °C.
A student who thinks the respirometer responds to carbon dioxide picks this. In fact carbon dioxide is absorbed by the alkali, so the reading reflects oxygen uptake, which genuinely fell.

mcqs.q: In one reaction of the Krebs cycle, two hydrogen atoms (each with an electron) are removed from a substrate and accepted by NAD. Which statement describes this reaction?
options: The substrate is reduced and NAD is oxidized by the transfer.
Neither substance is oxidized, because no oxygen takes part in it.
The substrate is oxidized, but NAD only holds hydrogen and is unchanged.
The substrate has been oxidized and NAD has been reduced.
mcqs.specStatementText: Oxidation is losing hydrogen; NAD carries it
mcqs.explain: Oxidation is loss of electrons. Removing hydrogen with its electron (dehydrogenation) oxidizes the substrate, and NAD, which accepts the hydrogen, is reduced; the two occur together as a redox reaction.
rationales: A student who attaches the labels the wrong way round picks this. In fact the substrate loses hydrogen and electrons, so it is oxidized; NAD gains them, so it is reduced.
A student who defines oxidation as gain of oxygen picks this. In fact oxidation is loss of electrons, so dehydrogenation is an oxidation whether or not oxygen is present.
A student who thinks a carrier is a passive container picks this. In fact a redox reaction always involves both changes: NAD accepts the hydrogen and is reduced to reduced NAD.

Oxidation is loss of electrons. Removing hydrogen with its electron (dehydrogenation) oxidizes the substrate, and NAD, which accepts the hydrogen, is reduced; the two occur together as a redox reaction.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly summarises the stages of glycolysis?
options: Glucose is phosphorylated using ATP, split into two three-carbon molecules that are oxidized, and ATP is then formed.
Glucose is phosphorylated, forming ATP, and then split into two pyruvate molecules that are reduced.
A single enzyme splits glucose directly into two pyruvate molecules, releasing energy in the form of ATP.
Glucose is split into two pyruvate molecules without any oxidation, as no oxygen is present in the cytoplasm.
mcqs.specStatementText: Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate, step by step
mcqs.explain: Glycolysis involves phosphorylation of glucose (using ATP), lysis into two three-carbon molecules, oxidation of these by removal of hydrogen to reduce NAD, and formation of ATP; each step has its own enzyme.
rationales: Glycolysis involves phosphorylation of glucose (using ATP), lysis into two three-carbon molecules, oxidation of these by removal of hydrogen to reduce NAD, and formation of ATP; each step has its own enzyme.
A student who assumes any phosphorylation makes ATP picks this. In fact phosphorylation of glucose uses ATP, and the three-carbon molecules are oxidized, not reduced.
A student who mistakes the summary equation for the mechanism picks this. In fact glycolysis is a stepwise pathway in which each reaction is catalysed by a different enzyme.
A student who thinks oxidation needs oxygen picks this. In fact the three-carbon molecules are oxidized by dehydrogenation, reducing NAD, even though no oxygen is involved.

mcqs.q: During glycolysis of one glucose molecule, two ATP are used in phosphorylation and four ATP are formed later. What is the net yield per glucose?
options: A net gain of 4 ATP as well as 2 reduced NAD
A net gain of 2 ATP together with 2 reduced NAD
A net gain of 6 ATP plus another 2 reduced NAD
A net gain of 2 ATP together with 2 oxidized NAD
mcqs.specStatementText: Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate, step by step
mcqs.explain: Four ATP formed minus two ATP used gives a net yield of two ATP. The oxidation steps also produce two reduced NAD, and two pyruvate are formed.
rationales: A student who counts only the ATP-forming steps picks this. In fact two ATP were used to phosphorylate glucose, so the net gain is 4 − 2 = 2 ATP.
Four ATP formed minus two ATP used gives a net yield of two ATP. The oxidation steps also produce two reduced NAD, and two pyruvate are formed.
A student who thinks phosphorylation of glucose produces ATP adds 2 + 4 and picks this. In fact the phosphorylation step consumes ATP, so the net gain is two.
A student who reverses the redox labels picks this. In fact NAD accepts hydrogen during the oxidation steps and so becomes reduced NAD.

mcqs.q: During intense exercise, muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate. What is the purpose of this conversion?
options: To release extra ATP from pyruvate once the mitochondria have stopped working.
To oxidize pyruvate so that more reduced NAD is available to the cell.
To regenerate NAD so that glycolysis can continue producing ATP.
To convert pyruvate into a form able to enter the mitochondria.
mcqs.specStatementText: Making lactate keeps glycolysis running without oxygen
mcqs.explain: Reducing pyruvate to lactate converts reduced NAD back to NAD. This allows glycolysis, which needs NAD for its oxidation step, to continue with a net yield of two ATP per glucose.
rationales: A student who thinks lactate formation is where the anaerobic ATP comes from picks this. In fact no ATP is formed in this step; all the ATP comes from glycolysis.
A student who assumes every step of respiration is an oxidation picks this. In fact pyruvate is reduced, accepting hydrogen from reduced NAD, which is thereby oxidized back to NAD.
Reducing pyruvate to lactate converts reduced NAD back to NAD. This allows glycolysis, which needs NAD for its oxidation step, to continue with a net yield of two ATP per glucose.
A student who thinks all respiration passes through mitochondria picks this. In fact lactate formation occurs when oxygen is insufficient and the mitochondrial pathway cannot be used.

mcqs.q: How does anaerobic cell respiration in yeast differ from anaerobic cell respiration in human muscle?
options: Yeast uses a different pathway from glucose to pyruvate, with its own distinct set of enzymes.
Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol only, since carbon dioxide cannot form without oxygen.
There is no difference: both convert pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide when oxygen is absent.
Yeast regenerates NAD by turning pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide, not lactate.
mcqs.specStatementText: Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide instead
mcqs.explain: The pathways are the same as far as pyruvate. Yeast regenerates NAD by decarboxylating pyruvate and reducing the product to ethanol, so the final products are ethanol and carbon dioxide rather than lactate.
rationales: A student who infers different pathways from different products picks this. In fact glycolysis is identical in yeast and humans; only the NAD-regenerating step differs.
A student who thinks carbon dioxide needs oxygen picks this. In fact yeast decarboxylates pyruvate, releasing carbon dioxide, before reducing the product to ethanol.
A student who applies the yeast equation to humans picks this. In fact human muscle reduces pyruvate directly to lactate, with no carbon dioxide released.

The pathways are the same as far as pyruvate. Yeast regenerates NAD by decarboxylating pyruvate and reducing the product to ethanol, so the final products are ethanol and carbon dioxide rather than lactate.

mcqs.q: Yeast is used in baking to make dough rise and in brewing to make beer alcoholic. Which statement explains both uses?
options: Anaerobic respiration of sugars produces carbon dioxide, which raises the dough, and ethanol, which remains in the beer.
The carbon dioxide that raises dough comes from aerobic respiration, since anaerobic respiration releases none.
Yeast produces lactate, as human muscle does, which sours the dough and makes the beer alcoholic.
Yeast uses the small amount of oxygen dissolved in the dough or beer to produce carbon dioxide and ethanol.
mcqs.specStatementText: Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide instead
mcqs.explain: In anaerobic respiration yeast converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide. Bubbles of carbon dioxide make dough rise (the ethanol evaporates in baking), while the ethanol is the alcohol in beer.
rationales: In anaerobic respiration yeast converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide. Bubbles of carbon dioxide make dough rise (the ethanol evaporates in baking), while the ethanol is the alcohol in beer.
A student who generalises from human anaerobic respiration picks this. In fact yeast releases carbon dioxide anaerobically, by decarboxylating pyruvate, which is what makes dough rise.
A student who thinks all anaerobic respiration gives lactate picks this. In fact yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; lactate is not alcoholic and is not a yeast product.
A student who thinks anaerobic respiration uses a little oxygen picks this. In fact ethanol is produced only when oxygen is absent; the pathway needs no oxygen at all.

mcqs.q: What happens to pyruvate in the link reaction of aerobic cell respiration?
options: It enters the Krebs cycle directly, where it combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
It is oxidized and decarboxylated to a 2C acetyl group, which coenzyme A carries to the Krebs cycle.
It reacts with oxygen in the matrix, forming carbon dioxide and a two-carbon acetyl group that enters the cycle.
It is bound by coenzyme A, the enzyme that catalyses its conversion into citrate in the matrix.
mcqs.specStatementText: The link reaction turns pyruvate into a 2C acetyl group
mcqs.explain: In the link reaction pyruvate loses carbon dioxide (decarboxylation) and hydrogen (oxidation, reducing NAD) to form an acetyl group, which is bound to coenzyme A and transferred to the Krebs cycle.
rationales: A student who leaves out the link reaction picks this. In fact pyruvate (3C) is first converted to a 2C acetyl group; it is the acetyl group, not pyruvate, that joins oxaloacetate.
In the link reaction pyruvate loses carbon dioxide (decarboxylation) and hydrogen (oxidation, reducing NAD) to form an acetyl group, which is bound to coenzyme A and transferred to the Krebs cycle.
A student who thinks carbon dioxide is made by adding oxygen picks this. In fact the carbon dioxide comes from decarboxylation; oxygen is used only at the end of the electron transport chain.
A student who reads 'coenzyme' as 'enzyme' picks this. In fact coenzyme A is a carrier that accepts the acetyl group; the reactions are catalysed by separate enzymes.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the Krebs cycle is correct?
options: Oxaloacetate is used up in each turn of the cycle, so it must be supplied continually from pyruvate.
Most of the ATP from aerobic respiration is formed directly by the reactions of the cycle itself.
Citrate (6C) forms when an acetyl group (2C) joins oxaloacetate (4C), which is then regenerated.
Carbon dioxide is released when oxygen combines with the carbon atoms of citrate.
mcqs.specStatementText: The Krebs cycle oxidizes acetyl groups and regenerates oxaloacetate
mcqs.explain: Citrate is produced by transfer of the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate. The cycle's oxidations and decarboxylations then convert citrate back to oxaloacetate, ready for the next acetyl group.
rationales: A student who expects every reactant to be consumed, as in a linear pathway, picks this. In fact oxaloacetate is regenerated by the reactions of the cycle.
A student who sees the cycle as the main energy-releasing stage picks this. In fact the cycle forms only one ATP per turn; most ATP is made by chemiosmosis using the reduced NAD.

Citrate is produced by transfer of the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate. The cycle's oxidations and decarboxylations then convert citrate back to oxaloacetate, ready for the next acetyl group.
A student who thinks oxygen is a reactant of the cycle picks this. In fact carbon dioxide is released by decarboxylation; oxygen is used only as the terminal electron acceptor.

mcqs.q: One acetyl group enters the Krebs cycle and oxaloacetate is regenerated. Which account of one turn of the cycle is correct?
options: Two carbon dioxide molecules form when oxygen oxidizes the carbon atoms of the acetyl group directly.
Each of the four oxidations forms one ATP directly, so the cycle yields most of the cell's ATP supply.
Only decarboxylation occurs, since no oxygen enters the matrix to oxidize any of the cycle's intermediates.
Two decarboxylations give off carbon dioxide, four dehydrogenations reduce carriers, one ATP forms.
mcqs.specStatementText: The Krebs cycle oxidizes acetyl groups and regenerates oxaloacetate
mcqs.explain: Per turn, two carbons leave as carbon dioxide by decarboxylation, four oxidations by removal of hydrogen produce reduced carriers (mainly reduced NAD), and one ATP is formed directly.
rationales: A student who thinks oxygen reacts in the cycle picks this. In fact the oxidations are dehydrogenations and the carbon dioxide comes from decarboxylation, without any oxygen.
A student who attributes most ATP to the cycle picks this. In fact the oxidations reduce NAD; only one ATP per turn is formed directly, and most ATP comes from chemiosmosis.
A student who thinks oxidation needs oxygen picks this. In fact four oxidations occur in each turn by removal of hydrogen, which reduces NAD, with no oxygen involved.
Per turn, two carbons leave as carbon dioxide by decarboxylation, four oxidations by removal of hydrogen produce reduced carriers (mainly reduced NAD), and one ATP is formed directly.

mcqs.q: What is the role of reduced NAD in aerobic cell respiration?
options: It passes a pair of electrons to the first carrier of the electron transport chain, becoming NAD again.
It phosphorylates ADP directly in the matrix, so each reduced NAD becomes a fixed number of ATP.
It carries hydrogen from the Krebs cycle only, because glycolysis in the cytoplasm forms none.
It carries electrons across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space to build the gradient.
mcqs.specStatementText: Reduced NAD hands its electrons to the chain
mcqs.explain: Energy is transferred when reduced NAD passes a pair of electrons to the first carrier in the chain. This regenerates NAD, which returns to glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.
rationales: Energy is transferred when reduced NAD passes a pair of electrons to the first carrier in the chain. This regenerates NAD, which returns to glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.
A student who reads 'ATP equivalents' tables as a direct exchange picks this. In fact reduced NAD transfers energy to the electron transport chain, and ATP is made by chemiosmosis.
A student who forgets the earlier stages picks this. In fact reduced NAD is formed in glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle, and all of it feeds the chain.
A student who thinks electrons are what cross the membrane picks this. In fact electrons pass along carriers within the membrane; it is protons that are pumped into the intermembrane space.

mcqs.q: Isolated mitochondria are supplied with pyruvate and oxygen. A poison then blocks the first carrier of the electron transport chain, and the Krebs cycle also stops. Which statement explains why the cycle stops?
options: The poison prevents oxygen from reaching the matrix, so the cycle can no longer oxidize citrate to oxaloacetate.
Reduced NAD can no longer pass its electrons to the chain, so no NAD is regenerated for the cycle's oxidations.
Reduced NAD can no longer phosphorylate ADP directly, and the cycle runs on the ATP that this provides.
Oxaloacetate is no longer supplied by the chain, so citrate cannot form from the acetyl groups.
mcqs.specStatementText: Reduced NAD hands its electrons to the chain
mcqs.explain: The Krebs cycle oxidizes substrates by reducing NAD. NAD is regenerated only when reduced NAD gives its electrons to the first carrier; with that blocked, all NAD stays reduced and the dehydrogenations halt.
rationales: A student who thinks the cycle uses oxygen directly picks this. In fact oxygen is not a reactant in the cycle; the cycle stops because NAD, not oxygen, is no longer available.

The Krebs cycle oxidizes substrates by reducing NAD. NAD is regenerated only when reduced NAD gives its electrons to the first carrier; with that blocked, all NAD stays reduced and the dehydrogenations halt.
A student who thinks reduced NAD makes ATP directly picks this. In fact reduced NAD donates electrons to the chain; the cycle halts because NAD is not regenerated, not for lack of ATP.
A student who thinks oxaloacetate is consumed and must be resupplied picks this. In fact oxaloacetate is regenerated within the cycle; the chain does not supply it.

mcqs.q: How is the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane generated?
options: Protons are pumped from the intermembrane space into the matrix as electrons flow along the chain of carriers.
Hydrolysis of ATP supplies the energy needed to pump protons across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space.
Energy released as electrons flow along the chain pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space.
Electrons themselves are pumped across the inner membrane, leaving the protons behind in the matrix.
mcqs.specStatementText: Electron flow pumps protons across the inner membrane
mcqs.explain: As electrons flow from carrier to carrier along the electron transport chain, energy released at each transfer is used to move protons from the matrix across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space.
rationales: A student who places the proton build-up where ATP is made picks this. In fact protons are pumped out of the matrix into the intermembrane space, and flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase.
A student who thinks all active transport uses ATP picks this. In fact the pumping is powered by electron flow along the chain; this is the process that makes ATP, not one that uses it.

As electrons flow from carrier to carrier along the electron transport chain, energy released at each transfer is used to move protons from the matrix across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space.
A student who mixes up which particle crosses the membrane picks this. In fact electrons stay within the carriers; the energy they release is used to pump protons across.

mcqs.q: How does ATP synthase couple the proton gradient to the synthesis of ATP?
options: It hydrolyses ATP to pump protons across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space, building the gradient.
Water moves through it by osmosis into the matrix, and the resulting pressure change forces phosphate onto ADP.
Protons collect in the intermembrane space and phosphorylate ADP there, on the outer surface of the enzyme.
Protons flow through it down their gradient into the matrix, releasing energy that phosphorylates ADP.
mcqs.specStatementText: Protons flow back through ATP synthase, making ATP
mcqs.explain: ATP synthase is the route by which protons diffuse back into the matrix. The energy released as they move down the gradient is coupled to joining phosphate to ADP: this is chemiosmosis.
rationales: A student who takes ATP synthase for another pump picks this. In fact ATP synthase does not pump; protons flow through it passively and it makes ATP.
A student who reads 'chemiosmosis' as osmosis of water picks this. In fact it is protons, not water, that move through ATP synthase, down their concentration gradient.
A student who places ATP synthesis where the protons accumulate picks this. In fact protons pass through the enzyme into the matrix, and ADP is phosphorylated on the matrix side.
ATP synthase is the route by which protons diffuse back into the matrix. The energy released as they move down the gradient is coupled to joining phosphate to ADP: this is chemiosmosis.

mcqs.q: A chemical makes the inner mitochondrial membrane freely permeable to protons. Electron flow and oxygen consumption continue, but ATP synthesis stops. Which statement explains these observations?
options: Protons leak back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, so no gradient remains to drive ADP phosphorylation.
Electrons leak through the membrane instead of reaching oxygen, so no energy arrives at ATP synthase.
Water enters the matrix by osmosis, diluting the ADP and phosphate so that they can no longer be joined together.
Reduced NAD cannot transfer energy directly to ADP, because the leak removes the protons that it needs.
mcqs.specStatementText: Protons flow back through ATP synthase, making ATP
mcqs.explain: Chemiosmosis needs a proton gradient and a single route back through ATP synthase. If protons can cross the membrane anywhere, the chain still pumps them (so electron flow and oxygen use continue) but no gradient builds up and ATP synthase has nothing to drive it.
rationales: Chemiosmosis needs a proton gradient and a single route back through ATP synthase. If protons can cross the membrane anywhere, the chain still pumps them (so electron flow and oxygen use continue) but no gradient builds up and ATP synthase has nothing to drive it.

A student who thinks electrons cross the membrane picks this, but it contradicts the data: oxygen is still consumed, so electrons are still reaching it. Electrons stay in the carriers; it is protons that leak.
A student who reads chemiosmosis as osmosis picks this. In fact water plays no part; ATP synthesis fails because the proton gradient has been dissipated.
A student who thinks reduced NAD phosphorylates ADP directly picks this. In fact reduced NAD gives electrons to the chain, and the electron flow is unaffected; only the gradient is lost.

mcqs.q: What is the role of oxygen in aerobic cell respiration?
options: It combines with carbon atoms from the acetyl group in the Krebs cycle to form the carbon dioxide released.
It accepts electrons from the final carrier of the chain and protons from the matrix, forming water.
It is not needed for the chain to run; it is used only in the last step to form water.
It oxidizes glucose directly in the cytoplasm, converting it to pyruvate in glycolysis.
mcqs.specStatementText: Oxygen takes the electrons at the end of the chain
mcqs.explain: Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor. By accepting electrons from the last carrier and protons from the matrix it forms metabolic water and keeps the carriers oxidized so that electron flow continues.
rationales: A student who thinks the carbon dioxide is made from the oxygen picks this. In fact carbon dioxide comes from decarboxylation; the oxygen consumed becomes water.

Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor. By accepting electrons from the last carrier and protons from the matrix it forms metabolic water and keeps the carriers oxidized so that electron flow continues.
A student who sees water formation as a minor finishing step picks this. In fact without oxygen to accept electrons the final carrier stays reduced and the whole chain stops.
A student who thinks oxidation means adding oxygen picks this. In fact glycolysis oxidizes the sugar by removing hydrogen to NAD; oxygen is used only at the end of the chain in the mitochondrion.

mcqs.q: A student claims: 'Without oxygen the electron transport chain keeps running; only the formation of water stops.' Which statement correctly evaluates this claim?
options: Correct: the chain needs only reduced NAD to keep running, and oxygen is required just to make water.
Incorrect: the chain stops because the Krebs cycle needs oxygen to keep supplying it with reduced NAD.
Incorrect: with no terminal acceptor the final carrier remains reduced and electron flow stops.
Incorrect: the chain stops because without oxygen there is no ATP to power the proton pumps.
mcqs.specStatementText: Oxygen takes the electrons at the end of the chain
mcqs.explain: Each carrier can pass electrons on only if the next one is oxidized. Oxygen keeps the final carrier oxidized by accepting its electrons; without oxygen the carriers back up in the reduced state and flow ceases.
rationales: A student who treats oxygen's role as a trivial last step picks this. In fact allowing continued flow of electrons is precisely oxygen's role; without it the chain, proton pumping and chemiosmosis all stop.
A student who thinks the Krebs cycle uses oxygen directly picks this. In fact the cycle stops for lack of NAD, which is a consequence of the chain stopping, not the cause of it.

Each carrier can pass electrons on only if the next one is oxidized. Oxygen keeps the final carrier oxidized by accepting its electrons; without oxygen the carriers back up in the reduced state and flow ceases.
A student who thinks the pumps are driven by ATP picks this. In fact proton pumping is driven by electron flow itself; the chain stops because there is nothing to accept the electrons.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly compares lipids and carbohydrates as respiratory substrates?
options: Carbohydrates yield more energy per gram, because they are the body's main and most readily used fuel.
Lipids yield more energy per gram, because they contain more oxygen atoms that can be oxidized.
Lipids can be respired without oxygen once their fatty acids have been converted into glucose.
Lipids yield more energy per gram, as they have less oxygen and more oxidizable hydrogen.
mcqs.specStatementText: Lipids give more energy per gram but need oxygen
mcqs.explain: Fatty acids are less oxidized than sugars: they contain little oxygen and more hydrogen and carbon per gram that can be oxidized, so more reduced NAD is formed and more ATP is made per gram.
rationales: A student who confuses how readily a fuel is used with how much energy it holds picks this. In fact lipids yield roughly twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates.
A student who links 'oxidation' with oxygen content picks this. In fact lipids contain less oxygen; their higher yield comes from more oxidizable hydrogen and carbon.
A student who thinks every substrate is turned into glucose picks this. In fact fatty acids are broken down to acetyl groups that enter via acetyl-CoA, so they can be respired only aerobically.
Fatty acids are less oxidized than sugars: they contain little oxygen and more hydrogen and carbon per gram that can be oxidized, so more reduced NAD is formed and more ATP is made per gram.

mcqs.q: A sprinter's leg muscles rely on anaerobic respiration during a 100 m race. Which statement explains why the muscles cannot use fatty acids to supply this energy?
options: Fatty acids enter aerobic respiration as acetyl-CoA and cannot enter glycolysis, the only stage that yields ATP without oxygen.
Fatty acids must first be converted into glucose, and this conversion is far too slow to keep pace with a sprint.
Fatty acids can be respired anaerobically, but the muscle prefers glucose because it is much faster to break down.
Fatty acids contain too little energy per gram to supply the very large amount of ATP that a sprint needs.
mcqs.specStatementText: Lipids give more energy per gram but need oxygen
mcqs.explain: Glycolysis and anaerobic respiration occur only if carbohydrate is the substrate. Fatty acids are converted to acetyl-CoA and oxidized in the Krebs cycle, which depends on the electron transport chain and therefore on oxygen.
rationales: Glycolysis and anaerobic respiration occur only if carbohydrate is the substrate. Fatty acids are converted to acetyl-CoA and oxidized in the Krebs cycle, which depends on the electron transport chain and therefore on oxygen.

A student who thinks all substrates are turned into glucose picks this. In fact fatty acids are not converted to glucose in muscle; they enter respiration as acetyl-CoA, which requires the aerobic pathway.

A student who thinks any substrate can be used without oxygen picks this. In fact fatty acids cannot be respired anaerobically at all, because they bypass glycolysis and enter only the aerobic pathway.

A student who thinks carbohydrate is the richer fuel picks this. In fact lipids hold roughly twice the energy per gram; the problem is that releasing it requires oxygen, which the sprinting muscle lacks.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic C1.2 Cell respiration

Hydrolysing ATP releases energy; making it takes energy in
Respiration makes ATP inside cells; gas exchange is something else
Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans compared

Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate, step by step
Making lactate keeps glycolysis running without oxygen
Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide instead
The link reaction turns pyruvate into a 2C acetyl group

scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept or rationale quotes a value in kilojoules per mole for ATP hydrolysis. Items test only the direction of the energy transfers and the idea that the energy released per ATP is enough for many tasks in the cell.

Glycolysis is described only as phosphorylation, lysis, oxidation and ATP formation with 'three-carbon' molecules; no intermediate (hexose bisphosphate, triose phosphate, etc.) is named anywhere in the file.

Only citrate and oxaloacetate are named. No other Krebs cycle intermediate appears, and the four oxidations are counted without naming the second hydrogen carrier (FAD), which the 2025 guidance does not require and which the reported 2028 revision removes.
Electron carriers are referred to only as 'the first carrier', 'carriers' or 'the final carrier'; no complex is numbered or named (no Complex I-IV, cytochrome c or ubiquinone).

omitted.sequence: no authored ordering; would require inventing a sequence
